newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Coffee price pleases Brazil growers, worries trade.
newsitem.headline: Coffee price pleases Brazil growers, worries trade.

text.p: The buying frenzy which has seized the world's coffee markets is making Brazilian producers very happy and Brazilian traders rather worried about the impact of prices on consumption, dealers said.

"This is an historic moment - but also a worrying one. These prices could start to hit consumption as housewives may start buying smaller quantities," said Jorge Esteve, president of the Brazilian Coffee Exporters Association (Abecafe).

On Wednesday, the New York benchmark July contract peaked at $2.97 a lb, the highest price since September 1977, and Brazilian traders were now expecting to see the contract break the psychological $3 a lb level on Thursday.

The current rally is just the latest in a series of price rises since the start of this year but one key difference for Brazilians is that internal prices are also rising, with traders quoting sales Wednesday of fine coffee at 300-310 reais per bag.
This compares with prices in the middle of this month of around 260 reais a bag and 240 reais at the end of April.

Dealers attributed the firmer internal market to a tightening in domestic supply. Old crop coffees were coming to an end and the thin flow of coffee from the new crop has been reduced to a trickle because of the rains this week.

For producers the high prices are doubly sweet as they have only before seen these levels when the Brazilian crop has been hit by weather problems and they therefore have had less to sell, dealers said.
"There's a producer meeting going on in Patrocinio (Minas Gerais) and everyone is laughing. The only news is how many producers have now got Mercedes," one trader said.

Most traders expected to see some profit-taking once the July contract pierces $3 a lb but then they expected prices to pick up steam again through winter with the ever-present concern about excessively cold weather in the country's coffee regions.

But a frost-free winter should see prices begin to slip back after September and once supplies from Central American nations start to filter through towards to the end of the year, traders said they expected to see New York prices fall back to between $1.70 to $2 a lb.
